newsitem.title: USA: Reuters Asset Allocation Poll (New York) Sept 3.
newsitem.headline: Reuters Asset Allocation Poll (New York) Sept 3.

text.p: Money managers slashed allocations to U.S. debt markets in the past two months amid a tide of expansionary U.S. economic data, according to a new Reuters survey of fund managers and investment strategists.
Debt fund managers cut U.S. bonds to 20 percent of assets in August, down from 27 percent in June, the survey said.
Bond market fears of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike made foreign debt more attractive, these money managers said.

"The market is starting to price in some fear of a rate move again," said Brian Gendreau, a market strategist at J.P. Morgan. "There's about a 50-50 chance (the Fed) will move in September and about an 80 percent chance they'll move at the November meeting."
Debt strategists who cut back on U.S. allocations said the Fed would raise rates in response to recent signs of faster economic growth.
Last Thursday, the Commerce Department revised its estimate of second-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth to 4.8 percent from 4.2 percent.
Economists said the high final sales and low inventories components of the GDP report suggest growth remains strong in the third quarter.

"We were expecting to see signs of the U.S. economy slowing down," said Keith Wirtz, senior vice president and director of global investment management at Bank of America. "That number caught us off guard."
Recent reports on consumer confidence, jobless claims and weekly retail sales were strong as well.
In light of recent reports, "the data just before the Fed decided not to hike rates (in August) was an aberration," said Gendreau.

Debt portfolio managers freed funds from the United States and Japan to spread them into European markets, according to the survey. German debt received the greatest influx, rising to 16 percent of total assets from 11 percent in June.
"The German yield curve is very steep now," Gendreau said. You can get out of the United States, buy Germany and hedge back into dollars and pick up 250 basis points."
Allocations also upticked for certain European high-yield markets and for the Canada/Australia/New Zealand survey category.
Volatile stock prices caused equity fund managers to cut their U.S. allocations in the past two months as well, to 29 percent of total assets from 33 percent.
"When we saw the market move back to the levels we're sitting at, we felt it was time to reduce our exposure," said Bank of America's Wirtz.

Wirtz said he cut U.S. equities to 25 percent of total allocations from 30 percent in June as foreign markets became "Because foreign central banks have been in an easing posture, growth is going to accelerate down the road," Wirtz explained. "We see an investment opportunity in non-U.S. markets over the next one to two years."
Wirtz increased his holdings of Japanese stocks using funds culled from German allocations.
"Japan is becoming a focus, but we're optimistic on Europe as well," Wirtz said.
Besides pruning U.S. shares, other survey respondents cut back in Japan and other Asian countries while adding to Germany and non-core Europe.
